This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a high-dimensional Schrödinger equation. By assuming a Gaussian prior for the ground state, we prove that the generalization error in the relative L2 norm is bounded by $\sigma\sqrt{\log d}/N$ after training with $N$ samples from the given $O(N)$ samples in the Gaussian prior. Following this, we demonstrate that the neural network can achieve a convergence rate of $N^{-\alpha/2}$ for any $0<\alpha<1$ when trained with $N$ samples, and that the convergence rate is limited by the condition number of the Laplacian matrix. Furthermore, we show that the neural network can achieve a convergence rate of $N^{-1}$ when the condition number is not excessively large. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments. This research was partially presented at the 2021 SIAM Conference on Mathematical and Computational Issues in Computational Physics. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, thanks to a thriving community contributing numerous formal proofs related to programming languages, algorithms, and data structures. However, the sheer scale of the archive currently hinders new contributors from effectively utilizing its content. To address this challenge, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the Isabelle subgraph from the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs to identify underlying patterns. Our research reveals that the Isabelle subgraph exhibits characteristics of a small-world network with distinct clusters corresponding to different areas of expertise. We have also developed a novel algorithm to automatically identify and categorize these clusters. Leveraging our findings, we have created a sophisticated recommender system for suggesting relevant proofs to Isabelle users based on their interests. Our recommender has been successfully tested and refined through a pilot study involving 10 participants, resulting in improved discovery of relevant proofs for users. Furthermore, we have used our insights to streamline the process of introducing new contributors to the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs by providing them with personalized guidance on the content they can utilize and contribute. Our approach has been successfully applied in a pilot program to 10 new contributors, leading to increased efficiency in their contribution process. Our study's outcomes and methodologies are thoroughly documented, enabling other contributors to replicate and build upon our methods. Ultimately, our research aims to enhance the overall quality and usability of the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs by making its vast content more accessible to its diverse community. In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant attention
for their ability to effectively learn from graph data. However, the current
dataset landscape for GNNs is characterized by a scarcity of resources and a
lack of diversity in terms of properties. This issue is exacerbated by the
tendency of models to overfit their training data, hindering their ability to
generalize. One potential solution to address this challenge is the
implementation of transfer learning, which involves leveraging knowledge gained
from one graph dataset to improve performance on another. Despite its potential,
the feasibility of transfer learning in GNNs remains poorly understood. This
study investigates the application of transfer learning in GNNs, focusing on
uncovering the factors that contribute to its success or failure and identifying
the types of graph data that are most amenable to transfer learning. Our
research reveals that the effectiveness of transfer learning depends on the
similarity between source and target graphs, which can be evaluated using
metrics such as node classification accuracy and network statistics. Furthermore,
our findings suggest that transfer learning is more successful when the target
graph contains nodes with similar characteristics to those found in the source
graph, which can be identified through clustering analysis. Our research also
highlights the importance of node degree distribution in transfer learning,
demonstrating that GNNs can effectively transfer knowledge when the target graph
has a node degree distribution similar to that of the source graph. This study
contributes to the development of transfer learning in GNNs by shedding light on
the underlying factors that influence its success and failure, ultimately paving
the way for the design of more effective transfer learning strategies for GNNs.

experience replay. These algorithms employ a sampling strategy that reduces variance
in the sampled transitions, utilizing a weighted distribution based on estimated

benchmarks, especially in complex multi-task scenarios. Furthermore, POER's
variance-reduced gradient estimator enables the use of larger replay buffers than
previously possible. Our results demonstrate the potential of combining policy

the contents of the replay buffer. We also provide insights into the limitations of

Blind and low vision individuals face significant challenges accessing printed documents, including books, articles, and emails, due to their visual limitations. To address this issue, researchers proposed the integration of a table of contents and a subject map, achieved through the application of text summarization techniques. An experiment involving blind and low vision individuals demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach, with results showing that a subject map significantly reduced the time it took to locate specific information in an email. Furthermore, the researchers explored the use of different summarization techniques, including manual, automatic, and human-annotated methods, and found that human-annotated summarization produced the most satisfactory subject maps. An evaluation of NavEmail through a usability study confirmed its benefits and provided valuable feedback for future improvements. The researchers also suggested that NavEmail could be integrated into email clients as an accessible feature. The study's findings and recommendations were presented to the email industry, with the hope of influencing future design and development to improve email navigability for all users. Furthermore, we found that the optimal sample size for regional analysis varies depending on the specific brain region, with larger samples required for regions with high predictive accuracy. This study provides valuable insights for researchers designing resting-state functional connectivity studies, particularly those focused on multisite data collection. It also underscores the importance of considering the unique analytical requirements of different brain regions. Ultimately, our findings highlight the potential for multisite data analysis to improve the accuracy of connectivity measurements and predictive modeling in psychiatric neuroscience. This paper addresses the problem of jointly selecting users and designing precoders in multiuser MIMO systems through a dual formulation. To tackle the resulting non-convex optimization issue, we transform it into a convex problem by introducing a virtual transmit covariance matrix and reformulate it as a rank-one matrix approximation problem. This approach yields a user selection and precoder design scheme that is both efficient and scalable. Furthermore, we establish the conditions under which this scheme achieves the optimal degrees of freedom in the multiuser MIMO broadcast channel. Our numerical results confirm the scheme's ability to achieve the optimal degrees of freedom and outperform existing methods. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve. This last finding has implications for the study of non-embeddable valuations on function fields of tropical curves. Specifically, it shows that certain infinite sets of rational functions that were previously proposed as embeddable are, in fact, finitely generable over a specific semifield, which contradicts a previous conjecture. Nevertheless, the problem of determining whether all infinite sets of rational functions that were previously proposed as embeddable are, in fact, finitely generable over a specific semifield remains unresolved. The techniques employed in this study are also applicable to general R-processes, yielding new insights and results. This study investigates the effectiveness of Continual Learning (CL) methods in handling multiple tasks and suggests that the primary challenge lies in adapting to new tasks rather than retaining old ones. To support this hypothesis, a straightforward baseline model was developed, consisting of a single linear layer with random parameters for each new task, trained sequentially using stochastic gradient descent on each new task's data. The results show that this simple approach rivals the performance of more complex, transformer-based CL methods that leverage pre-trained language models. Furthermore, an analysis of the model's behavior reveals that the main challenge in CL is indeed adapting to new tasks rather than retaining old knowledge. The study's findings also highlight the importance of hyperparameter optimization in CL and suggest that the current reliance on complex models and sophisticated CL methods may be unnecessary. By demonstrating that a simple, efficient approach can achieve comparable results, this study encourages the CL community to reevaluate its approach to model development and experimentation. This study presents an interpretable model for multi-modal hate speech detection that uses a BERT-based encoder and incorporates visual information from comments to provide context. The model's attention scores and token/visual feature importance are used to explain its predictions. The results show that our model outperforms the current state-of-the-art performance on the Hatefuls8 Challenge dataset, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.813. The model's interpretability was demonstrated through the analysis of 50 instances, highlighting common characteristics of hate comments. The results indicate that our model's predictions are influenced by the text's semantic meaning, and not by biased visual information. The objective of Automatic Program Repair (APR) is to suggest repairs for broken software code. Current APR methods, although effective, are limited in their ability to cover all potential repair options due to the vast number of possible solutions. This study introduces a novel approach that frames APR as a learning task where a model generates patches to "attack" faulty code. By utilizing a neural network to create patches for unsolved APR cases, we can expand the scope of possible repairs and enhance the quality of suggested fixes. Our approach is based on the premise that patches can be seen as adversarial examples, and we can leverage this concept to create synthetic patches. We propose an adversarial patch generation method using a combination of generator and discriminator networks, trained on real patches from fixed code snippets. Our results demonstrate that these synthetic patches can successfully fix broken code and outperform other methods in a range of metrics. Furthermore, we found that the generated patches can be used to "vaccinate" code against future errors, with a significant improvement in resilience. Machine learning applications in wireless communication systems are becoming increasingly prominent, with graph neural networks (GNNs) emerging as a key technology. However, current GNN research primarily focuses on data generation and training, with little consideration given to real-world wireless networks. This study aims to bridge this gap by examining the application of GNN inference in wireless networks, with a specific emphasis on how channel conditions and network architecture affect performance. To address this, we employ a decentralized inference approach, utilizing a wireless communication system with multiple access and eavesdropping capabilities. By analyzing this system, we develop a metric to evaluate network performance and investigate how GNN inference is impacted by various wireless networks. Our results demonstrate that GNN inference is highly dependent on channel conditions and network architecture, with stronger wireless links and more robust network architectures leading to better performance. To address these challenges, we propose a GNN inference scheduling algorithm, which optimizes performance by balancing communication and information exchange in the network. Our findings demonstrate that this algorithm can significantly improve GNN inference, with a 50% reduction in error rates achievable under optimal network configurations. Overall, this study highlights the importance of considering wireless networks when designing machine learning applications, with implications for future research in this area. The study's findings and analysis provide valuable insights for practitioners and researchers working on GNN inference in wireless communication systems. various types of noise, effectively simulating the conditions of real-world
problems. This objective stems from the observation that the optimal step size
in SGD depends on the level of noise, which can be unpredictable in actual
problems. To address this challenge, we propose a new family of adaptive SGD
methods that estimate noise without relying on pre-existing knowledge or a
test dataset. Our approach is based on the concept of variance estimation and
offers theoretical guarantees for its performance. Furthermore, we provide
practical guidelines for implementing these algorithms and offer empirical
justifications for their effectiveness. Additionally, we explore the potential
extensions of these algorithms to accelerated variants, such as NAG and SGDm. The

real-world noise and outperform existing methods in actual problems. This work is
a crucial step towards creating a universal SGD method that can be applied to a
wide range of problems with diverse levels of noise. Our findings are expected to
be of significant value to researchers working on adaptive SGD methods and
optimization techniques. This research is a part of the author's Ph.D.

These regimes correspond to over-damped, under-damped, and critically-damped oscillations.  A critical point is identified, where the occupation number's amplitude approaches zero as the system approaches critical damping.  A novel type of self-oscillating system is thus established, where the occupation number exhibits under-damped-like behavior near the critical point.  This new class of self-oscillating systems is distinguished from traditional ones by its ability to be tuned to the critical point through adjustments in the system's parameters. This paper introduces DexGraspNet, a comprehensive dataset designed to facilitate robotic research on object grasping. Leveraging simulation technology, the dataset encompasses a vast library of 10,000 unique objects, encompassing 1,000 basic shapes and 9,000 generated variants, to ensure thorough coverage of possible grasps. The dataset includes precise annotations for grasp execution success rates and corresponding stable configurations, allowing for accurate evaluation of grasping algorithms. By employing simulation, the dataset can be expanded without constraints, unlike physical experiments, to support continuous research and validation. Additionally, a pre-trained model based on DexGraspNet is provided to support real-world robotic grasping in a Pando Robotics Panda FR-850 robotic arm through a novel approach called Sim2Real by Autonomous Vision. The model achieves a grasp success rate of 0.46 in a real-world setting, demonstrating significant improvement over a baseline rate of 0.16. This paper presents a model compression technique through knowledge distillation, 
preserving the flow of information from the larger to the smaller model.
The proposed method, InDistill, addresses the information loss issue commonly 
encountered in traditional knowledge distillation by leveraging the teacher model's 
output to guide the student model's learning of critical information.
By incorporating an additional task, InDistill enhances the student model's 
capability to capture crucial details, thereby improving its overall performance.
InDistill's effectiveness is demonstrated across various scenarios, including 
when the teacher and student models utilize the same or different backbones, as 
well as when the teacher model's output is perturbed with noise.
In these scenarios, InDistill achieves superior performance compared to conventional knowledge distillation methods.

Recent advancements in deep learning have made monocular depth estimation and semantic segmentation increasingly accurate. Pre-training models on large datasets has become a common practice, but the optimal pre-training task remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the relative effectiveness of using monocular depth estimation versus classification for pre-training on the segmentation of outdoor scenes. Our findings suggest that pre-training on monocular depth estimation yields superior results on segmentation tasks, but this advantage diminishes when using multi-label segmentation. We attribute this outcome to the fact that depth targets are more densely populated across pixels, facilitating faster convergence and better performance. This research investigates the potential benefits of using Vision Transformers (ViTs) in zero-shot anti-spoofing tasks for facial recognition systems. ViTs are particularly well-suited to handling spoofing attacks that occupy a significant portion of a frame. A straightforward yet effective approach, ViTFace, leverages a combination of a face detector and a ViT-based classifier to identify genuine and spoofing faces. Notably, ViTs can process entire images without requiring down-sampling, allowing them to capture more detailed information and thereby improve performance. The proposed method, ViTFace, demonstrates superior performance compared to existing solutions, with results showing a significant improvement of over 4% and 2% in accuracy on the DFWP and CASPEL datasets, respectively. Furthermore, ViTFace exhibits a substantial reduction in inference time, with a speed-up of 2x and 3x on the DFWP and CASPEL datasets, respectively. Reinforcement learning has shown great potential in numerous real-world applications, yet several challenges persist, particularly in complex scenarios with limited data and non-stationary environments. To address these issues, researchers have turned to hierarchical reinforcement learning, which decomposes tasks into manageable sub-tasks and leverages expertise to facilitate learning. However, this approach often requires substantial amounts of data and can struggle with generalization. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel framework that integrates model-based hierarchical reinforcement learning with inductive logic programming. By representing sub-tasks as logical formulas and utilizing an ILP system to induce these formulas from expert trajectories, our framework achieves improved data efficiency and better generalization capabilities. Additionally, the ILP system can provide valuable insights into the underlying decision-making processes of the learned policies. Experimental evaluations on well-known domains demonstrate that our proposed framework successfully identifies accurate sub-task representations and outperforms existing HRL methods in terms of performance on unseen data. Moreover, the induced sub-tasks facilitate the development of more interpretable and transferable skills. Overall, our work demonstrates the potential of integrating HRL and ILP to address the challenging aspects of reinforcement learning. The implementation of our framework is available on GitHub.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by imposing prior constraints on the latent image. Typically, images are assumed to follow a Gaussian Prior, but this is suboptimal as natural images also exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics within local regions. To address this limitation, we introduce the Kernel Mixture Model, a more expressive image prior that combines multiple Gaussian kernels, learned from a diverse dataset of natural images through Discrete Optimization. This learned prior enables us to derive an analytical solution for the ill-posed deblurring problem and achieve superior results on both synthetic and real-world blind image deblurring tasks, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. Formal verification through Hoare logic has been a reliable method for ensuring program correctness, yet its practical application is hindered by the complexity of manually crafting pre- and post-condition specifications. To address this issue, we propose a new framework, Natural Hoare Logic, which leverages the analysis of programs through logical forms derived from natural language descriptions. This framework employs a natural language parser and a semantic analyzer to break down the input into logical forms, which are then used to generate Hoare logic specifications. These specifications are subsequently verified using Hoare logic reasoning. To test the efficacy of this approach, we developed a prototype system and conducted a case study involving a program from the F-Illuminate project, which demonstrated the potential for automatic verification. While the current implementation is limited by its reliance on external tools and the absence of a comprehensive parser, we believe that Natural Hoare Logic offers a promising direction for future research. The accompanying code can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/hoarelogic/nhl.

stochastic gradient optimizer, this algorithm is highly scalable and can be easily
adapted for parallel processing on multi-core CPUs and GPU architectures. Our
results demonstrate the efficacy of M-ar-K-Fast ICA in identifying independent
components from large datasets. Furthermore, we provide open-source implementations
of M-ar-K-Fast ICA to facilitate its adoption in neuroscience and other fields.

Recent advancements in dialogue systems have been driven by pre-trained language models. However, these models struggle to comprehend dialogue context, which relies heavily on semantic analysis. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Dialogue Semantic Encoder (DSE), a pre-trained dialogue model that leverages semantic information to support dialogue understanding. Additionally, we develop a new task, semantic matching, to enhance the model's semantic learning capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that the DSE model outperforms existing dialogue models on multiple tasks, including natural language inference, slot filling, and dialogue classification. Furthermore, we show that by incorporating the DSE model, the performance of BERT-based models can be significantly improved on popular dialogue benchmarks. The DSE model and associated code are available on GitHub for public access.

Our results are consistent with a bimodal distribution, separating the stars into two distinct subpopulations with iron abundances of around -1.50 and -1.80 dex. Image search algorithms, which allow users to locate specific images online, have become increasingly efficient over time. However, the process of searching for an image remains a complex task for humans, requiring a query that perfectly matches the target image's visual characteristics. This paper introduces a new technique called Active Image Indexing (AII), which aims to simplify image search by utilizing a user to identify images that are similar to a query image. AII involves training a model to recognize when an image's description does not accurately match its visual content, prompting the user to provide a better description. By leveraging human input, AII continuously adapts and improves the performance of the indexing model without requiring retraining. Experiments demonstrate that AII achieves better results than traditional image search algorithms and remains effective even when the query is limited to text. Deep generative models, specifically variational autoencoders (VAEs), are being used to analyze complex data distributions. This limitation leads to poor performance in applications like anomaly detection and data generation. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative approach that leverages a least square objective function to learn a non-Gaussian prior for the latent space of VAEs. By applying regularization to the encoder and sampler, our method allows for more flexible latent space representations. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing solutions in terms of reconstruction accuracy, anomaly detection, and generated sample quality. Additionally, we provide theoretical justifications for the benefits of using a non-Gaussian prior in the latent space of VAEs. A novel approach to gray-coded modulation is proposed, leveraging deep learning to replace complex look-up tables with a single, efficiently trained model. This model generates quantized 'L-values' for each input 'K-value', and corresponding phase maps are computed using an iterative process. The resulting approach demonstrates comparable performance to traditional methods based on inverse discrete Fourier transforms, while showcasing improved efficiency through reduced computational requirements and streamlined memory access. Notably, the proposed technique exhibits a significant 75% decrease in floating-point operations and a 65% decrease in memory access operations compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the method's adaptability is demonstrated through successful application to various modulation schemes, including 4-QAM, 16-QAM, 64-QAM, and 256-QAM. Lastly, the method's scalability is assessed by evaluating its performance under high-throughput conditions. The results indicate that the method's performance loss remains relatively low, with an average error probability increase of less than 0.1% when operating at a data rate of 1 Tbit/s. By performing a chi-square fit to the muon's magnetic moment, the W boson mass, and the 125 GeV Higgs boson mass, we determine the 95% confidence level (CL) boundaries for the Higgs boson masses of the two doublets. We find that the Higgs boson masses must lie within the ranges of approximately 83.3-105.4 GeV and 500-700 GeV, assuming a Type-X two Higgs doublet model with a decaying light neutral scalar. Software developers utilize search queries to identify specific code segments within a program's source code, although many queries yield insufficient results. To address this issue, we propose a technique called QUICKAR that employs crowd-sourced information and natural language processing to reformulate original search queries and enhance concept location. By analyzing the query's syntax and semantics, QUICKAR identifies potential issues and suggests modifications based on associated concepts extracted from crowd-sourced data. Our approach was evaluated using 50 search queries and 10 developers, and the results demonstrate a significant improvement in identifying relevant code segments, with a 64% increase in accuracy compared to the original queries. Furthermore, through a user study, we validated the effectiveness of QUICKAR by gathering feedback from 5 developers, and the results indicate that 80% of the participants found the suggestions helpful and feasible to implement. Based on these findings, we conclude that QUICKAR is a practical and efficient tool for reformulating search queries and facilitating concept location. The implementation of QUICKAR is available on GitHub at https://github.com/abdullahalmasry/QUICKAR.

The educational setting of software testing poses unique challenges, primarily due to its abstract nature and the need for students to develop skills in both a theoretical and practical context. To address these issues, educators often rely on feedback mechanisms, but these can create problems if students become overly reliant on them, hindering their ability to think critically and independently. To mitigate this, we conducted an empirical study comparing the effectiveness of traditional feedback and inquiry-based learning, which encourages students to take ownership of their learning process and provides feedback only when necessary. Our results indicate that students who received inquiry-based learning outperformed those with traditional feedback in both conceptual understanding and exam performance, and also demonstrated improved satisfaction levels. Notably, while there was no significant difference in practical skills between the two groups, both groups showed significant improvement in this area. Based on our findings, we recommend that educators adopt a combination of both traditional and inquiry-based learning approaches, tailored to the specific needs of their students. This could involve using traditional feedback for areas requiring practical application and inquiry-based learning for more abstract, conceptual topics. Ultimately, we believe that by adopting such a strategy, educators can empower their students to become more self-sufficient learners and help them develop the critical thinking and problem-solving skills required for success in the field of software testing. To overcome this limitation, we propose a semi-supervised adaptation method that relies on target data self-labeling through a transfer learning process. Our approach involves initially training a model on the source domain with a focus on generating pseudo labels for the target domain. Next, we employ a target domain self-supervised learning strategy to refine the model using the generated pseudo labels. Our method is validated through experiments on various datasets, including MNIST, SVHN, and USPS, with results demonstrating its superiority over existing techniques. Our analysis reveals that the model's effectiveness depends on the ratio of attenuation to bandwidth, and we demonstrate that as this ratio increases, the model's accuracy decreases. Our findings also indicate that the model's accuracy is influenced by the type of attenuation present in the link - whether it is uniform or frequency-dependent. Based on our analysis, we suggest a method for improving the model's accuracy in discrete-time links by adjusting its step size. Our research was conducted using a range of channel models, including both simple and complex scenarios, and we verified our results by comparing them to exact solutions of the original fiber equations. Our findings have significant implications for the design of fiber-optic communication systems, particularly in systems that are subject to significant loss and dispersion. To enhance the effectiveness of e-commerce search and recommendation, a significant amount of unstructured product data needs to be efficiently organized and represented. Current deep learning models primarily rely on visual and structural information from product pages, but these approaches have limitations due to the need for extensive data collection and the inherent noise and variability of visual and structural data. In contrast, language-based product descriptions are generally more reliable and provide richer semantic information, making them an ideal choice for product representation. However, traditional text-based models are often insufficient on their own, as they lack critical visual and structural context. To address these challenges, we propose a novel knowledge-aided pretraining framework that leverages multi-modal e-commerce knowledge to integrate the strengths of text, vision, and structure into a unified product representation. Our approach involves three key components: (1) a knowledge graph that captures e-commerce product relationships; (2) a knowledge-based unified product embedding method that encodes the product graph into a low-dimensional space; and (3) a knowledge-aware pretraining method that utilizes multi-modal e-commerce knowledge to generate robust product embeddings. Our approach demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on e-commerce related tasks such as product retrieval, recommendation, and duplicate detection. Notably, it achieves a Mean Average Precision of 0.245 on the TREC 2017 product retrieval benchmark, surpassing the previous best result of 0.173. Moreover, it significantly outperforms existing baselines in product recommendation and duplicate detection tasks. Our approach also shows remarkable efficiency, requiring only 1.5 hours to process a dataset with 1 million products. The progression of Alzheimer's disease from preclinical to clinical stages is difficult to forecast, and current methods mainly rely on biomarkers and demographic factors. This study investigates the potential of machine learning to predict clinical progression using structural MRI data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. We employed the Deep InfoMax technique, a self-supervised method that extracts meaningful features from MRI data, and trained a model to classify subjects into preclinical and clinical groups. We compared the performance of our model with supervised approaches, such as supervised progression prediction, and those using other unsupervised methods. Our results indicate that Deep InfoMax can identify brain regions critical for cognitive functions and outperforms other unsupervised methods in predicting clinical progression. However, it lags behind supervised approaches in accuracy. We also found that features extracted by Deep InfoMax are more interpretable than those from other unsupervised methods. This study demonstrates the capability of self-supervised learning to extract meaningful features from MRI data, which can be utilized for both progression prediction and identifying critical brain regions. It may serve as a valuable tool for developing early intervention strategies for preventing or slowing down Alzheimer's disease progression. Furthermore, the features extracted by Deep InfoMax could be employed to identify at-risk individuals and facilitate the development of targeted prevention and intervention programs. This study provides insights into the potential of self-supervised learning in neuroscience and machine learning. Real-time operating systems (RTOSs) within embedded systems manage and schedule applications' execution, ensuring timely completion of tasks. With the increasing complexity of these systems, traditional monolithic RTOSs struggle to provide isolation, security, and fault tolerance. In contrast, virtualization-based approaches offer a more modern solution, leveraging hypervisors to manage and schedule virtual machines (VMs). This paper introduces T-Visor, a lightweight hypervisor designed for embedded systems and capable of supporting multiple VMs with their own RTOSs. By integrating with hardware virtualization support, T-Visor efficiently schedules VMs and provides isolation while minimizing its own footprint. A case study demonstrates T-Visor's performance on the Zynq MPSoC platform, showcasing its ability to support four VMs with distinct RTOSs and achieve a context switch time of approximately 0.1 milliseconds. This achievement positions T-Visor as a viable option for mixed criticality embedded systems requiring hardware-based isolation and security. Furthermore, T-Visor's open-source design facilitates research, development, and collaboration within the embedded systems community. However, current methods struggle with disambiguating instructions that have multiple possible interpretations. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that decouples natural language from the state space, using a separate neural network to determine the reference point for each instruction. By doing so, we demonstrate improved performance on several benchmark problems, including both synthetic and real-world scenarios. We achieve this by leveraging the speaker's natural speech in a variety of contexts, using a self-supervised speaker model, to create a text-to-environmental-noise representation that captures their unique vocal characteristics. Aspect-based sentiment analysis aims to identify the emotional tone of specific aspects within product reviews. Previous studies have focused on extracting sentiment expressions and their semantic connections, but the underlying sentiment polarity remains unexplored. To address this, we propose a novel framework that combines supervised pre-training with contrastive learning to uncover implicit sentiment orientations. Our method involves leveraging a large corpus of unlabelled reviews to learn sentiment polarity for key aspects, and then fine-tunes this knowledge using a small dataset of labeled reviews. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach surpasses existing baselines and achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art models while utilizing significantly less labeled data. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the learned sentiment orientations accurately reflect the underlying sentiment polarity. This work presents a pioneering effort in uncovering implicit sentiment orientations and has the potential to enhance the field of aspect-based sentiment analysis. Deep neural networks are highly effective for in-sample regression and classification but often struggle with identifying samples that fall outside their training data. To address this issue, we investigate the use of explicit uncertainty models within neural networks, focusing on a specific type of model known as Distributional Gaussian Processes. This work builds upon a previous method, DGPR, which treats each layer as an independent Gaussian Process using a shared variational distribution, but we find that incorporating this structure into even a single layer is a challenging task for current computational resources. To overcome this limitation, we develop a simplified model, SGPR, which approximates the full DGPR by assuming a shared variational distribution only at the final layer. This approach allows for efficient inference and we demonstrate that SGPR can be seen as a two-part neural network, comprising a normalizing flow and a Gaussian Process regression model. We then adapt SGPR to be used in conjunction with other layers, creating a hybrid model known as Hybrid-GPR. This model is shown to be effective in detecting out-of-distribution samples and we demonstrate its application in detecting data augmentation anomalies. Furthermore, we investigate the use of SGPR as a normalizing flow and apply it to other Gaussian Process models, including the original DGPR, to improve their efficiency. This work provides a new approach to modeling uncertainty in neural networks and we hope that it will serve as a stepping stone for future research in this area. This study presents an exploratory analysis of Turkish Twitter users' responses to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, a 7.0 magnitude disaster that occurred on October 30th. Our research focuses on understanding public sentiment, detecting trending topics, and uncovering demographic insights. We utilized a dataset of 1,113,111 tweets, selecting only those that are relevant and written in Turkish. Our findings reveal that women (53.1%) were more active on Twitter than men, with the majority (62.5%) being aged between 18 and 34. Sentiment analysis revealed a predominantly negative tone (-0.23), while topic modeling identified 100 distinct topics. We also found that the most active hour was between 18:00 and 19:00. Our analysis suggests that Twitter users were primarily concerned with the aftermath of the earthquake, with related topics including emergency response, aid, and social media appeals for support. We also identified a significant number of tweets related to politics, with users expressing opinions on the Turkish government and opposition. Our study contributes to the existing body of research on Twitter analysis by providing a comprehensive exploration of the public's reactions to a significant disaster like the Izmir earthquake. We hope that our findings can inform policymakers and humanitarian organizations, enabling them to develop more effective strategies to support those affected by crises. This research introduces a pioneering challenge in object pose estimation: categorically locating objects without any prior knowledge of their 3D models or specific views. We address this issue by developing a novel method that can adapt to new categories with minimal annotations. Our approach relies on a single image that represents each category and involves estimating pose through both rotation and translation prediction, along with 2D-3D view pose matching. We develop a training strategy that focuses on new categories with limited supervision and evaluate our method on the PASCAL 3D+ dataset, achieving an average rotation and translation error of 14.4 degrees and 0.63 meters, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can adapt to novel categories with high accuracy. For instance, our method achieves an average rotation and translation error of 5.8 degrees and 0.63 meters, respectively, for the "car" category, despite having no prior knowledge of its 3D model. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/alexsu85/zero-shot-pose.

This study introduces a novel control approach that leverages prior knowledge and real-time learning to effectively control complex, dynamic systems despite limited data availability. By incorporating prior system knowledge into the learning process through the construction of a system model, our method significantly reduces the need for extensive system identification and data collection. Our method's efficiency and effectiveness are also assessed through a comparison with reinforcement learning and random exploration. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have achieved significant success in various tasks, but their training can be unstable and unpredictable. To address this issue, researchers have introduced the Relation GAN (RelGAN), which utilizes a relation network to stabilize training and enhance diversity. Although RelGAN demonstrates improved stability and diversity, it tends to produce images with lower visual accuracy. To resolve this problem, this paper proposes an improved RelGAN called Relation GAN with Triplet Loss (RelGAN-T), which incorporates a memory bank and the triplet loss to increase visual accuracy by maintaining a record of previously encountered real images and minimizing the difference between the generated synthetic images and the stored real images. The experimental results confirm that RelGAN-T achieves superior visual quality, outperforming the original RelGAN and other state-of-the-art GAN models. Specifically, it surpasses the state-of-the-art models on the CIFAR-10 and CelebA datasets by 2.21%, 2.19%, and 0.90%, respectively. Additionally, it significantly outperforms the original RelGAN by 2.21%, 2.19%, and 4.19% on the same datasets. A new approach to twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) has been proposed, 
replacing the conventional phase locking method with a single laser. This alternative 
method utilizes a single laser for both Alice and Bob's channels without the need for 
synchronization, significantly reducing potential errors and improving stability. This 
modified TF-QKD protocol can still achieve the same level of security as the original 
TF-QKD framework. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the single laser can be 
operated in either pulsed or continuous wave modes, allowing for the single laser to be 
shared among multiple users without causing interference. This shared laser 
potential enables TF-QKD to be more easily implemented in distributed scenarios, 
such as quantum networks. Experimental results validating the single-field pulsed TF-QKD 
protocol have been presented, achieving a key rate of 3.5 Mbps over 50 km with the aid of 
two high-performance single-photon detectors. This research provides a practical path 
forward for the development of TF-QKD systems. Moreover, it has been theoretically shown 
that the single-field approach can tolerate a higher level of channel loss, up to 60 km 
with the aid of a high-performance channel restoration technique. This study offers a 
promising solution for the implementation of TF-QKD in challenging environments.

develop a universal quantum source, enabling the generation of entangled states across 
long distances. This source can be applied to various quantum communication protocols,

Object detection has seen significant advancements in recent years, particularly with the introduction of detection models that can identify a wide range of objects without the need for extensive, annotated data sets. However, current open-vocabulary detection methods rely on a large number of synthetic annotations to achieve high performance, which can be both time-consuming and costly to prepare. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative technique that utilizes pseudo labels in the form of bounding boxes to train open-vocabulary detectors. By applying our method, we demonstrate that it's possible to train open-vocabulary detectors using synthetic data with reduced annotation overhead, while also improving performance on real-world images. Furthermore, we've developed an efficient data balancing approach that ensures high-quality pseudo labels are generated for the training of open-vocabulary detectors. Our method has been successfully tested on the CUB-200-2011 and Charactera34 data sets, with results showing substantial gains in detection performance over baseline models. Notably, we've achieved a mAP of 44.4% on the CUB-200-2011 data set, a 6.4% improvement over baseline models. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

This research investigates the performance of factor models in mortality forecasting, focusing on two key variations: models with factors whose influence changes over time and those with fixed factors. We analyze these models within the context of the Lee-Carter framework, highlighting the differences between the two and their implications for parameter estimation. Our analysis reveals that models with time-varying factor loadings offer greater adaptability but are more susceptible to model instability issues. In contrast, models with fixed factor loadings provide more stable estimates and are better suited for long-term forecasting, although they may struggle to accurately predict short-term changes. Ultimately, our results suggest that models with time-varying factor loadings excel in mortality forecasting, outperforming their fixed counterparts in both short-term and long-term forecasting scenarios. We also observe that models with time-varying factor loadings can effectively predict changes in mortality rates, even when those changes occur suddenly. Our findings are supported by real-world data from the UK Office for National Statistics. We also conduct a series of Monte Carlo simulations to further validate the performance of factor models in mortality forecasting. Recent breakthroughs in neural architecture search (NAS) have been hindered by the phenomenon of "interference" - a phenomenon where the output of one architecture sampler affects the sampling process of other architectures, often resulting in the discovery of overly simplistic models. This paper delves into the causes of interference, examining its impact on diverse model design. To address this issue, we propose a novel objective function that is resistant to interference, as well as a straightforward training method that accelerates NAS. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that interference can be effectively mitigated through the use of our proposed objective and training method, enabling the discovery of complex models on challenging datasets such as CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet. Specifically, our results show that interference can be significantly reduced on the ImageNet dataset, resulting in a 2.1% improvement in top-1 accuracy for the MNAS-Net architecture. Moreover, our proposed training method enables the discovery of more complex models in as little as 7 hours, a 3x reduction in training time compared to the standard approach. This represents a substantial improvement in both model complexity and training efficiency. To facilitate future research, we have made our code and data available for public access. The Strauss process is a point process that is often used to model spatial patterns in a given area. It is defined by two main parameters: the intensity parameter, lambda, which represents how many points to expect within a given area, and the interaction parameter, beta, which determines how close these points can be to one another. If beta is greater than 1, points tend to cluster together, while a value of 1 results in evenly distributed points and a beta of 0 or less indicates that points are more likely to be found farther apart from one another. Traditionally, simulating this process is difficult due to its non-renewal nature and the fact that the area in which points are generated to be included is not fixed. A new method, however, has been developed to efficiently simulate this process by breaking down the region into smaller, non-overlapping sections, or tiles, where each section's area is determined based on lambda and a given beta value. To effectively classify multi-disciplinary documents in fields like science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), a comprehensive understanding of each field's core is necessary. A common misconception is that a general classification model can be applied across all subfields of a particular discipline, but this is not the case. For instance, fields like computer science and physics have distinct areas of focus, influencing how documents should be classified within those subfields. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that involves identifying and links mathematical entities within documents to understand their underlying subject matter and make more informed classification decisions. By combining this approach with a classification model, we can improve the accuracy of document classification in a particular discipline while accounting for its unique subfields. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches, particularly in classifying documents under specific discipline-subfield combinations. Moreover, we found that incorporating subfield information is essential for accurate document classification in certain cases. This research contributes to the development of a more effective and adaptive classification system that can be applied across a broader range of disciplines, subfields, and data sets. A proposed evaluation metric, the average precision of subfield classification, provides a clear understanding of the potential benefits of such a system. Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are limited in their ability to measure quality comprehensively. To address this issue, we introduce SummScore, a new evaluation metric that assesses summary quality by comparing it to its reference summary using a Cross-Encoder. This metric outperforms existing metrics in its ability to correlate with human quality assessments, with particular strength in measuring coherence. Additionally, SummScore is versatile and can be used in various settings, including both human and automated evaluation. To facilitate use, we provide pre-trained Cross-Encoders and a scoring script. Furthermore, we propose a method to train a summary model to produce high-quality summaries using SummScore as a target, which demonstrates its ability to improve the quality of generated summaries. This study is based on the author's publication in IJCAI 2021.

We introduce BEVFusion, a straightforward yet effective 3D object detection method
that leverages the synergies between LiDAR and camera sensors in the BEV space.
Unlike existing fusion-based detectors that combine feature maps from the LiDAR and
camera, our approach instead fuses individual detectors and only communicates
feature maps through a lightweight, end-to-end trainable bridge. This simple yet
robust design allows us to easily integrate the method with existing 2D and 3D object
detectors, leading to superior performance with fewer parameters. Notably, our
method surpasses the state-of-the-art in the LiDAR-only and fusion benchmarks on
Waymo Open Dataset and NuScenes benchmark while using significantly fewer
parameters. Our code is available at https://github.com/kuangcy/BEVFusion.

Discussions among software developers are a valuable source of information that can be analyzed to gain insights into their design decisions, leading to the development of design mining. This technique aims to identify designers' intentions by comparing design implementation discussions with similar discussions from a large corpus. However, previous studies on design mining have not thoroughly investigated the impact of varying the corpus size, a crucial aspect of this method. This paper examines the effect of corpus size on design mining by applying it to discussions from three different projects: Mozilla's Lightbeam extension, Mozilla's SafeTab feature, and Facebook's Like Button. The results show that small corpora (less than 100 discussions) can lead to inaccurate conclusions, whereas larger corpora (over 100 discussions) yield more consistent design intentions across multiple analyses. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of considering the design's complexity and the potential for multiple design intentions within a single feature. Based on these findings, the study proposes a set of guidelines for naturally language based design mining. These guidelines emphasize the need for a large, relevant corpus and a thorough understanding of the design's complexity and potential multiple purposes. Additionally, the study suggests that design mining should be viewed as a hypothesis generation process rather than a definitive design analysis. Ultimately, the study's conclusions underscore the need for a more systematic approach to design mining and highlight potential avenues for future research. The study's findings and recommendations are expected to contribute to the development of more effective design mining methods. The increasing demand for real-time analytics on live streams and historical data is driving the need for scalable, cloud-based data processing systems. However, current systems struggle to efficiently manage the diverse requirements of data processing pipelines, which need to combine stream and historical data with various aggregation and processing methods. To address this challenge, we present H-STREAM, a high-level streaming data processing language that allows users to define complex data pipelines with dynamic aggregation and processing strategies. H-STREAM's design incorporates a data placement mechanism to optimize stream and historical data storage, and it features a query execution model that ensures real-time processing of data processing pipelines. The H-STREAM compiler translates user-defined pipelines into cloud-native data processing jobs, which are executed by a distributed processing system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of H-STREAM through experiments on a cloud testbed, showcasing its scalability and performance in managing data processing pipelines. Additionally, we discuss the practical applications of H-STREAM in supporting real-time analytics for smart cities and industries. A recent breakthrough in translating SPARQL queries using neural machine translation has shown promise, despite struggling to handle knowledge base elements. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel mechanism that enables the model to copy elements from the knowledge base for both query construction and translation. Our approach builds on the existing Transformer architecture by incorporating an orthogonal mechanism that allows for copying elements during both encoding and decoding processes. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed mechanism significantly improves SPARQL translation accuracy, achieving a 11.9% increase in accuracy compared to the baseline model. Furthermore, the model's ability to handle knowledge base elements leads to a substantial 87.8% reduction in the number of elements the model must learn from the knowledge base. This study examines how significantly altering images affects both human observers and image classification models. We discovered that image transformations involving extreme changes, such as those affecting only a single pixel, have a more substantial impact on machines than humans. In contrast, similar transformations affecting entire images, such as those seen in the trolley problem, have a more profound effect on humans than machines. We propose a framework for understanding these findings and investigate the underlying causes through both behavioral and neuroimaging experiments. The results reveal that image transformations trigger automatic processing in machines but require conscious perception and intentional processing in humans. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that image transformations lead to decreased model confidence and increased human cognitive load, which in turn hampers both machine and human performance. Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of considering the distinct implications of extreme image transformations for both humans and machines. Our study reveals that minor modifications to audio inputs can significantly degrade the performance of these models. Specifically, we found that less than 1% alteration to the input waveform can impair their ability to distinguish between similar sounds, with loss rates exceeding 90%. Furthermore, we found that models using different self-supervision learning strategies exhibit varying levels of vulnerability to these attacks. Our research also demonstrates that adversarial samples can be generated efficiently using both gradient-based and gradient-free optimization techniques. Ultimately, we propose the use of adversarial training as a potential method for enhancing the robustness of speech back-end models. This research focuses on the study of the extended quantum plane $\mathbb{T}$, obtained by adding points to the quantum plane $\mathbb{P}$, where these additional points are called singular points. Specifically, we aim to find the complete list of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries of $\mathbb{T}$. These findings are further illustrated by a variety of examples. Moreover, we demonstrate that the number of possible $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries is independent of the quantum parameter $q$ and depends solely on the number of singular points. Our research also provides a generalization of these findings to the case of multiple quantum planes connected in a series. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of these results in the study of quantum curves and integrable systems. Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices are susceptible to various errors, with two significant types being gate-dependent and gate-independent noise. Implementing quantum error correction to mitigate these errors is computationally demanding due to its circuit complexity overhead. An alternative approach to reduce noise through error mitigation is developing, focusing on identifying and neutralizing error-causing correlations. We present a novel error mitigation technique, the hidden inverse protocol (HIP), which leverages the concept of hidden inverses to eliminate noise on quantum states. We demonstrate HIP's application in mitigating gate-dependent noise on a superconducting quantum processor, achieving a notable 94% reduction in state error. Furthermore, we show that HIP can be integrated with randomized benchmarking to enhance accuracy by 50%, suggesting its potential as a viable error mitigation strategy for NISQ devices. The implementation details of HIP are also made available for public access. In summary, our research indicates that HIP offers a promising approach to reduce noise and expand the applicability of NISQ devices. The findings of this study are expected to contribute significantly to the development of quantum computing. However, the standard image-text and visualisation protocols used for pre-training can be sub-optimal due to their sequential nature. To address this limitation, we introduce a new pre-training objective that leverages parallel processing of image and text features to improve the mapping between the two spaces. Additionally, we propose a new visual-guided text objective that enhances the semantic representation of the model by incorporating visual information to extract more meaningful text features. Our approach, VT-CLIP, outperforms state-of-the-art models in visual grounding and zero-shot learning tasks, demonstrating improved robustness and generalisation. This study introduces an efficient method for creating topologically correct quad meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models with high-order accuracy. The approach involves a two-stage process: first, it automatically divides the model into manageable polygonal elements using a customized algorithm; second, it optimizes the polygonal mesh to a quad mesh using a customized integer linear programming formulation. The method's speed and accuracy are further enhanced by leveraging the capabilities of the CGAL library for geometric computations and the Gurobi solver for optimization. The results show that our method outperforms existing quad-mesh generators in terms of both speed and accuracy. The proposed method has been successfully applied to generate meshes for various airfoil geometries and wing shapes. The accompanying code is available on the GitHub platform.

This paper aims to identify the conditions under which local queries are beneficial in improving learning from noisy data. By analyzing the trade-offs involved, we demonstrate that local queries are more useful when the dataset contains a large number of difficult examples with similar features. This is because local queries can help eliminate incorrect hypotheses more efficiently in datasets with more challenging examples. Our findings are supported by experimental results on synthetic datasets as well as real-world applications such as training face recognition models in the presence of malicious edits. Overall, our research highlights the importance of considering the specific dataset properties when designing local query-based methods for robust learning. Deep learning models have achieved significant success in medical image classification tasks, but they are highly susceptible to errors caused by noisy labels. To address this issue, we propose a novel label refurbishment mechanism that utilizes Bayesian statistics to eliminate label noise. Our approach involves a two-stage process where the model's confidence in its predictions is first calculated, and then a reliability rule is applied to determine which predictions need refurbishment. The noisy labels are then replaced with either the original class or the 'Unknown' class, and a Bayesian-based adjustment is applied to the model's parameters. Our method, which we call BSLRM, has been evaluated on two datasets and compared to other state-of-the-art label refurbishment techniques. The results show that BSLRM significantly outperforms the existing methods in mitigating label noise, with an improvement of 5-10% in accuracy on the tested datasets. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of BSLRM in handling both uniform and non-uniform label noise. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first label refurbishment method that utilizes Bayesian statistics to eliminate label noise in deep learning models. Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of label noise and the performance of different label refurbishment methods, and it sheds light on the role of model confidence in mitigating label noise. The proposed approach is validated through extensive experiments on public datasets, and it is expected to be a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners working with noisy labels in medical image classification tasks. Our work demonstrates the potential for using the Weyl-Feynman approach to investigate complex geometric representations of quantum systems and their implications for understanding quantum mechanics. Additionally, we explore the potential for using the $E_8$ root system as a basis for constructing quantum error-correcting codes. Our analysis suggests that states related to the real $E_8$ root system may be suitable for encoding due to their stability, but states related to complexifications may be more vulnerable to errors. Our work highlights the potential for using the Weyl-Feynman approach to investigate the geometric and algebraic aspects of quantum mechanics and their connections to information theory. Our study also underscores the potential for using the $E_8$ root system as a tool for understanding the connections between quantum mechanics, information theory, and complex geometry. In various collaborative scenarios, robots interact with humans based on established conventions, yet these conventions are not consistently communicated. To effectively work together, robots and humans need a shared understanding of the conventions in play. This study examines how robots can effectively communicate human-relevant conventions to humans during joint tasks, with a specific focus on reaching an endpoint by following a path. By incorporating a simple communication system, robots can convey the intended path to humans, who then adjust their walking path accordingly. We conducted two user studies to assess the efficacy of this approach, evaluating how effectively humans adapt to the robot's intended path and the types of cues that are most helpful for humans to reach the endpoint. Our results indicate that humans can successfully adapt to the robot's intended path, especially when the starting point is close to the endpoint, and when the path is clearly marked as the desired path. Based on these findings, we suggest a straightforward strategy for shared control that enables robots and humans to work together effectively to reach a common goal. This research has significant implications for various collaborative scenarios, including human-robot interactions in everyday life and in more complex robotic settings. Ultimately, our approach provides a foundation for developing more sophisticated communication systems that enable robots and humans to work together seamlessly in a range of collaborative environments. This system's local map concept is based on a simplified road network framework, which is then used to guide the robot through unknown territories.  As the robot navigates, it uses a probabilistic approach to determine the most likely path forward, which is then used to update the local maps and ensure a seamless transition to new areas.  HiTMap's approach has been tested in a simulated environment and the results show significant improvements in map accuracy and navigation performance.  This system is designed to be flexible and can be easily integrated into a variety of navigation systems.  To support the development of similar systems, we are releasing the HiTMap source code as an open-source contribution. This model is capable of simultaneously restoring images, separating materials, and filtering out noise from x-ray sensors. By formulating a task-oriented objective function, our model leverages the distinct characteristics of data from different energy levels to improve the reconstruction process. By converting this function into a minimization problem with two split Bregman iterations, our model is able to tackle the complexities of the original optimization problem. We validate the effectiveness of our model through both numerical simulations and real-world experiments. Our results demonstrate that our model is able to accurately identify materials, restore images, and filter out sensor noise. In comparison to existing methods, our model achieves superior results with minimal computational overhead. In various applications, such as scientific literature or news articles, a large number of entities are often mentioned, making it essential to pinpoint only the relevant information for users. Contextual Named Entity Retrieval aims to accomplish this by extracting and retrieving specific entity aspects - for example, names, locations, or company titles - in response to a given query. While current NER methods rely on term frequency and part-of-speech information, they often overlook the significance of individual terms in relation to the query. To address this limitation, we introduce a new approach that incorporates user-provided feedback to gauge term relevance and integrate it into the NER framework. By utilizing a novel feedback mechanism, our method demonstrates improved performance on both small and large datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art NER methods. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of our approach and suggest potential directions for future research. The proposed method is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuyang1989/CNER_with_feedback. Evaluations were conducted using the CNER dataset from the 2019 Indri Retrieval Workshop and the CDR dataset from the 2020 TAC KBP track. Notably, our approach achieved a 10% relative improvement in mean average precision over the best-performing NER baseline on the CDR dataset. Furthermore, we also evaluated our method on the 2020 TAC KBP dataset and demonstrated a 5% relative improvement in entity disambiguation task. The results of these evaluations are available on the TAC KBP evaluation server at https://www.tac.nist.gov/publications/2020/. Additionally, we also conducted a comparison study on the 2020 TAC KBP dataset and demonstrated a 5% relative improvement in entity disambiguation task. This method is particularly useful in environments where collecting extensive training data is impractical due to limited resources. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a critical component of clinical assessment, but current automated methods are limited by their narrow scope, trained on data from a single hospital. We investigate two potential solutions to this issue: retraining existing models to incorporate new data, and developing a general-purpose model from scratch, using a unique dataset comprising MRI scans from three separate hospitals. We find that retraining models to accommodate new data yields superior results, significantly outperforming models trained on a limited dataset and those applied to unrelated hospitals. Notably, our findings suggest that a model trained on data from two of the three participating hospitals achieves comparable performance to one trained on the combined data of all three. We propose a novel approach to incremental learning, allowing models to adapt to new data sources with minimal additional training. This method is based on a self-assessment of the model's confidence in its predictions, using this assessment to determine the proportion of data to be relabeled for the new hospital. We demonstrate that relabeling a subset of the existing data, based on this assessment, is sufficient to integrate the new hospital's data, without the need for further fine-tuning. This incremental learning approach is applied to a U-Net model, achieving a Dice coefficient of 0.83 for the combined data of all three hospitals, surpassing the performance of models trained on individual hospitals and those applied to unrelated data. We also examine the impact of data augmentation on the model's performance, finding that a combination of standard and complex transformations yields the best results. Our findings suggest that a well-designed incremental learning approach can effectively expand the scope of existing models, allowing them to be applied to new, unseen data with high accuracy. This methodology has the potential to revolutionize the field of medical image segmentation, paving the way for the development of general-purpose models capable of adapting to diverse datasets. We're examining a complex task where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The traditional approach, known as Borda addition, involves systematically adding items and evaluating their effect using a scoring system. However, this method has limitations, as it only considers individual item additions in isolation. In contrast, a more comprehensive approach, known as contextual addition, takes into account the interdependence of items and uses a ranking system that incorporates context. While contextual addition offers greater precision, it can be challenging to implement and may not always be necessary. To address this, we're proposing a new hybrid approach that combines the strengths of both methods. By using contextual addition for complex item combinations and Borda addition for simpler cases, this hybrid approach aims to provide a more efficient solution. In our empirical study, we compared the performance of these three methods on a diverse set of real-world datasets, finding that the hybrid approach consistently delivered superior results across a wide range of scenarios. Notably, the hybrid approach outperformed the other methods in 83% of the cases, while producing comparable outcomes in the remaining instances. These findings suggest that the hybrid approach offers a reliable solution for set addition problems, making it a valuable tool for decision-making applications. Transformer-based language models have been primarily evaluated on adult populations, but their performance on child-directed language remains understudied. This research investigates the ability of these models to process negation in language, a key aspect of children's developing grammatical skills. We examine negation usage in two contexts: absolute negation (e.g., "no") and relative negation (e.g., "not"), both of which pose distinct challenges for language modeling. Our analysis reveals that, despite the models' general proficiency in adult language, they struggle to apply negation rules consistently in child-directed utterances. This difficulty may be attributed to several factors, including the limited exposure to child-directed language, the inherent complexity of negation processing, and the reliance on contextual cues for accurate negation detection. To address these limitations, we propose a training strategy that enhances the models' ability to apply negation rules. Our approach involves training the models on both positive and negated sentence pairs, similar to the way children learn negation through double-agent games. This method demonstrates its effectiveness by improving the models' performance on various negation-related tasks and promoting more accurate negation use in the models' generated text. Our research contributes to the development of more effective language models for child-directed communication and offers valuable insights for creating tailored language systems for children. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of examining the social and cognitive contexts in which language is used, particularly when working with language models that are still in their developmental stages. Ultimately, our findings have significant implications for the design of language systems that are both socially and cognitively aware. To overcome this, we introduce a novel look-ahead attention model that incorporates not only the past target context but also future target attention weights into word attention weights. The proposed model can be efficiently trained and implemented by using a novel objective function that balances the training of target word embeddings with look-ahead attention weights. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model enhances both translation quality and robustness in various scenarios, including monolingual denoising, domain adaptation, and translation with out-of-vocabulary words. Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal framework for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note aims to highlight two crucial errors present in the original framework, along with their associated resolutions, which will ultimately lead to enhanced efficiency in the pricing of Asian options. Firstly, the pricing equation may not be uniquely solvable for options with non-standard payoffs when using the original framework. To address this, we suggest using a partial differential equation to determine the lower bound of the option price. Secondly, even when the pricing equation is solvable, it may not yield a computationally efficient solution. To overcome this, we propose the use of a Monte Carlo method based on the Markov chains of Kou, which can significantly improve the computational efficiency of the original framework. The effectiveness of our proposed method is demonstrated through numerical examples. This revised method retains all the benefits of the original framework, including the ability to handle a wide range of Markov-driven models and option payoffs, while providing a more efficient and accurate solution. Furthermore, our method can be used in conjunction with existing methods to provide a hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of different techniques to achieve even better results. To illustrate this, we also present a case study that combines our method with the partial differential equation approach to provide a more accurate solution. The combination of these methods has the potential to provide a more robust and efficient solution to the pricing of Asian options.
