A crucial aspect of reversible steganography involves accurately detecting the embedded probability distribution of secret messages and accurately determining the transmission probability of carrier signals. To address this, we propose a novel framework based on Bayesian neural networks, consisting of an encoder and decoder modules. These modules are trained in tandem to ensure they work in harmony, with the encoder module acting as the inverse operation of the decoder module. To achieve this, we employ a novel loss function that minimizes the difference between the Bayesian neural network's output and input, as well as a symmetric correlation coefficient. Furthermore, we develop a method to quantify the uncertainty of the classification process. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach surpasses the current state-of-the-art in terms of payload capacity, with the uncertainty measurement also providing an effective means of verifying the integrity of the embedded secret messages. Moreover, the theoretical foundations of the reversible steganography problem are refined, with the embedded probability distribution and transmission probability of carrier signals redefined. To facilitate comparison, we introduce a reference steganography platform. The source code for this platform is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenXin-2020/Reversible-Steganography. We develop a novel algorithm, starting with an initial phase of adaptive exploration that yields a compact representation of the action set's gradient. Ontologies are extensively utilized for data annotation and EXIF data management, 
exhibiting both hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections among their terms.
Although numerous visualization tools exist for showcasing hierarchical relationships, 
visualizations of non-hierarchical connections are scarce, making it challenging for 
users to identify and explore these connections among annotated data sets.
To address this gap, we propose OntoPlot, a novel visualization tool that displays 
both hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections in an ontology, enabling users to 
easily explore and identify all terms associated with a selected concept, regardless 
of the existing hierarchy.
In a comparative study with existing visualization tools, OntoPlot demonstrated its 
superiority in visualizing non-hierarchical connections, while also efficiently 
visualizing hierarchical relationships.
The tool's effectiveness is further demonstrated through its application in analyzing 
EXIF data from the 2020 German Parliament election campaign. OntoPlot is available

This study introduces a novel semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition approach that combines CycleGAN with inter-domain loss techniques. By leveraging CycleGAN to generate synthetic speech data with a target speech distribution, we can utilize a speech-to-text model to produce text outputs that are then matched with the real target distribution using inter-domain loss. We explore the effectiveness of three types of inter-domain loss: adversarial loss, cycle consistency loss, and permutation-free loss. Experimental results on the CSJ dataset demonstrate that our proposed method significantly improves recognition accuracy, with a 9.8% gain over the baseline model using real data and a 5.6% gain with 10% synthetic speech data. Moreover, we observe that the permutation-free loss achieves the best performance among the three inter-domain loss methods. Additionally, we investigate the impact of varying the amount of synthetic data on ASR performance and find that our approach consistently outperforms the baseline even with a high proportion of synthetic data. Notably, we observe that the quality of the synthetic data generated by CycleGAN has a direct impact on ASR performance, with higher quality data yielding better results. Overall, our proposed method demonstrates the potential for generating high-quality synthetic data to improve semi-supervised end-to-end ASR systems. This study presents a novel approach to music enhancement through image translation and vocoding. Given that music is a complex, multi-dimensional audio signal encompassing pitch, rhythm, and other harmonic and timbre components, we employ a multi-task image translation technique to tackle different aspects of music enhancement simultaneously. Specifically, we utilize the U-Net architecture for noise removal and a WGAN-GP-based model for music denoising, and leverage the WaveNet model for high-quality music synthesis. To leverage the strengths of these models, we develop a multi-task image translation framework that enables the network to learn a common latent space, allowing us to leverage pre-trained models and achieve improved results. Furthermore, we introduce a vocoder to generate high-quality music samples, and our approach is evaluated on both clean and noisy music samples. The results demonstrate that our technique outperforms existing methods in both performance and visual and audio quality metrics. Notably, the code and implementation details are publicly available on the GitHub platform.

This research delves into the effects of imperfections in human throwing gestures. Based on these findings, the research proposes a novel approach to authenticating virtual characters by analyzing the release technique used. Deep Neural Networks are highly effective in text classification tasks, but they can be compromised by subtle word manipulations that alter their meaning. Our study introduces the concept of sibylvariant transformations - variations of words that maintain their semantic context - to identify and circumvent potential biases in DNN models. Through our analysis, we discovered that word2vec models are prone to producing these transformations, which we then utilized to develop a range of targeted attacks against leading text classification models. Our research also reveals that these attacks can be countered by incorporating diversity into the word embeddings used in DNN models. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the vulnerabilities and robustness requirements of text classification DNN models. The code for our research is publicly available on GitHub. Our research is the first to employ sibylvariant transformations in adversarial machine learning, which we believe can be applied to other NLP tasks to uncover additional insights. Meta-learning goals for adapting to new, unseen tasks efficiently are becoming increasingly prominent. Researchers have developed various algorithms to tackle this challenge, but most existing methods rely on empirical success stories rather than being grounded in theoretical frameworks. This study addresses this gap by designing a framework for meta-learning using linear representations in a controlled setting. By applying this framework, we derive sample and computational complexity results for two meta-learning algorithms: one based on second-order statistics and another involving spectral analysis. The findings provide a theoretical understanding of the benefits of meta-learning and establish a link between the proposed algorithms and traditional, inductive learning methods. Moreover, we demonstrate that our meta-learning algorithms can achieve comparable performance using significantly fewer samples compared to their inductive counterparts. The theoretical results are substantiated by empirical experiments in the overparameterized regime. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of meta-learning and provides a link between the sample-efficient learning paradigm and traditional, inductive learning methods. The results are applicable to a broader context beyond linear representations, as exemplified by the application of our methods to classification and causal inference tasks. This study investigates the practicality of utilizing knowledge distillation to create compact machine translation models using limited training data. It compares the stability of quantization and knowledge distillation approaches in low-resource settings. To achieve this, we developed a metric to measure the effect of compression on translation quality, and conducted a series of experiments using a machine translation dataset with varying amounts of training data. Our results indicate that knowledge distillation yields better results than quantization, and that both methods can significantly improve model performance with large amounts of training data, but their effectiveness declines in low-resource settings. Furthermore, we found that while quantization is relatively robust, knowledge distillation is highly dependent on the choice of teacher model and training data. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach that combines knowledge distillation with multiple teacher models, and demonstrates its potential for creating compact machine translation models using large pre-trained language models. Our findings highlight the need for further research on developing stable compression techniques for low-resource machine translation. The segmentation of tree-in-bud lesions in high-resolution CT scans of the lung is crucial for diagnosing early-stage infectious diseases and inflammation. However, creating a reliable dataset for this task is challenging and time-consuming. This study investigates how different image augmentation techniques can be used to decrease the required amount of labelled data for training a tree-in-bud lesion segmentation model. We discovered that a combination of rotations, flipping, and zooming, along with colour adjustments, is the most effective strategy, allowing us to decrease the necessary labelled data by 75% while maintaining a high level of accuracy. We also found that these methods can be used to improve the robustness of the model to imaging modalities other than high-resolution CT. Our findings suggest that image augmentation can be a valuable tool for creating training datasets for complex medical image segmentation tasks. This can be particularly useful in situations where labelled data are scarce and expensive to obtain. This study provides insights into the effectiveness of different image augmentation techniques and highlights the need for further research to increase the robustness of medical image segmentation models to various imaging modalities. The study's results are expected to contribute positively to the development of reliable medical image segmentation models despite the limitations imposed by data scarcity. Image description generation, a crucial aspect of computer vision, requires precise control to tailor descriptions for specific purposes like creating inclusive content. Current models are limited by their inability to adapt to such requirements, leading to inconsistent outputs. We present a novel, flexible image description model called PromptCap, which can be controlled by incorporating external signals, like prompts, to modify its output. By leveraging the Cyclic Self-Training strategy, PromptCap optimizes its performance on target prompts without compromising its original performance on the base prompt. Our model's effectiveness is demonstrated through high-quality descriptions generated in response to various prompts, even when the image content is not explicitly shown. We evaluate PromptCap's performance on both automatic and human evaluation metrics, including COCO caption metrics and human ratings of fluency and coherence. Our results indicate that PromptCap successfully adapmits to diverse prompts while maintaining its original image description capabilities. Moreover, we showcase its practical applications in creating inclusive descriptions. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/whaing/PromptCap.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are crucial for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently. Researchers have been investigating various methods of probabilistic forecasting that can capture the uncertainty in consumption data. This paper presents an approach to forecasting daily peak consumption at the distribution grid level by combining point forecasts with an aid of time series analysis. The proposed method involves two key components: a time series-based model that generates a large set of possible consumption paths, and a model that identifies the most accurate subset of these paths. The performance of this approach is evaluated using real-world data from a French distribution company, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in producing accurate probabilistic forecasts.
